This vignette demonstrates the `pmxhelpr` forest plot workflow for visualizing 
the univariate impact of covariate effects in a model on the integrated model
output (e.g. exposure metrics, response metrics, ratio to reference)

The pipeline mirrors the [VPC](vpc-workflow.html) and 
[dose-proportionality](doseprop-workflow.html) workflows with one additional 
upstream function for pre-processing of raw simulated output:

  + `df_forest_preprocess()`: reshapes raw simulation output into summary 
  metrics for aggregation into summary statistics for forest plotting
  + `df_forest()`: aggregates summary metrics into a class-tagged summary object
  + `plot_forest()`: dual-mode plotting function which can consume either
  the reshaped output of `df_forest_preprocess()` for one-step summary and 
  plotting or the class-tagged summary output of `df_forest()`.

```{r setup, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
options(scipen = 999, rmarkdown.html_vignette.check_title = FALSE)
library(pmxhelpr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts =  FALSE)
library(ggplot2, warn.conflicts =  FALSE)
```



# Background

A univariate forest plot is a graphical model application used to visualize the
impact of intrinsic and extrinsic participant factors (i.e., covariates) on 
integrated model outputs (e.g., exposure metrics, response metrics, ratios of 
exposure or response) under test conditions relative to reference conditinos.

The typical workflow involves establishing the "reference" virtual participant
(i.e., the vector of covariates at the reference level for each individual 
covariate) and unique "test" virtual participants differing in only one 
covariate value from the reference participant. 

The model is then applied to generate predictions under each scenario with 
uncertainty and/or variability arising from unique sets of fixed effects model 
parameters in each simulation sampled from the uncertainty in parameter 
estimation (i.e., sampled from a multivariate normal distribution with the mean
vector set to the vector of final fixed effects parameter estimates). 

The output from the simulation is a distribution of "typical" (fixed effects 
only) model outputs, from which the median (50th percentile) is interpreted
as the estimate of central tendency and quantiles (e.g., 2.5th-97.5th, 5th-95th)
are interpreted as the confidence interval around the central tendency (e.g., 
95% CI, 90% CI)

The bioequivalence criteria (0.8 to 1.25) provide a conventional reference 
range for interpretation of covariate impact on exposure. 



# Data

This vignette uses two internal datasets built using the internal `data_sad`
dataset and the internal PK model (`pkmodel`). 

  + `data_sad_pkforest_sim`: raw exposure metric simulation output for N = 500 
    replicates. Dosing of 200 mg once daily to steady state. Exposure metrics 
    are summarized to one row per covariate set (M) per replicate (N) resulting
    in a dataset of length M x N (6 covariate sets * 500 replicates = 3000). 
    Example input dataset for `df_forest_preprocess()`
    
```{r data-sim-glimpse}
glimpse(data_sad_pkforest_sim)
```

  + `data_sad_pkforest`: pre-processed simulated exposure metrics. Exposure 
    metrics are gathered from columns into rows resulting in a dataset of 
    are summarized to one row per covariate set (M) per replicate (N) per metric
    (K) resulting in a dataset of length M x N x K (6 covariate sets * 
    500 replicates * 8 metrics = 24000).Example output dataset from 
    `df_forest_preprocess` and example input dataset for `df_forest()`. 

```{r data-scenarios}
glimpse(data_sad_pkforest) 
```

Relevant variables in these datasets include:
  + `ID` identifies the unique covariate sets 
  (1 = reference, 2 = fed, 3 = 50 kg, 4 = 60 kg, 5 = 80 kg, 6 = 90 kg)
  + `SIM` is the replicate counter 
  + `metric` holds the the exposure metric names, which include both absolute 
  (`CMAX`, `CMIN`, `AUC`, `CAVG`) and test/reference ratios 
  (`CMAXRATIO`, `CMINRATIO`, `AUCRATIO`, `CAVGRATIO`)
  + `value` holds the exposure metric values
  + `cov_var` holds the name of the univariate covariate varied
  (`Reference`, `FOOD`, `WTBL`)
  + `cov_val` holds the value of the univariate covariate varied
  (`Reference`, `Fed`, `50 kg`, `60 kg`, `80 kg`, `90 kg`)
  + `is_ref` flags the reference rows

It also carries a `cov_level_ref` attribute naming each covariate's reference.



# Preprocessing with `df_forest_preprocess()`

`df_forest_preprocess()` is the entry point from a simulation output to the 
forest plot pipeline. It reads the scenario structure from the covariate columns
in the raw simulation output. 

Key arguments are as follows:

  + `data`: data.frame, simulation output dataset for processing
  + `metric_vars`: character vector, names of metric variables in `data`
  + `cov_vars`: character vector, names of covariate variables in `data`
  + `cov_val_ref`: named vector, covariate name: reference value pairs 
  defining the reference conditions
  + `cov_labels`: list, covariate value:label pairs or labeling function

```{r preprocess}
simsum <- df_forest_preprocess(
  data_sad_pkforest_sim,
  metric_vars   = c("CMAX", "CMIN", "AUC", "CAVG"),
  cov_vars      = c("FOOD", "WTBL"),
  cov_val_ref = c(FOOD = 0, WTBL = 70),
  cov_labels    = list(
    FOOD = c("0" = "Fasted", "1" = "Fed"),
    WTBL = function(x) paste(x, "kg")
  )
)
glimpse(simsum)
```

Every column that is not a metric passes through, so simulation inputs such as
`ID`, `WTBL`, `FOOD` and `DOSE` stay available for filtering and faceting 
downstream.

This function call is exactly how the shipped dataset `data_sad_pkforest` is 
built, so the two are the same frame. The rest of the vignette works from 
`simsum` to follow the workflow which would be used in a real worked forest 
plot workflow.

```{r preprocess-identical}
identical(simsum, data_sad_pkforest)
```

The reference rows are flagged by `is_ref` and labeled `Reference`. The 
reference labels are attached as an attribute, ready to pass to `df_forest()` 
as `cov_level_ref`. 

```{r preprocess-attr}
ref_levels <- attr(simsum, "cov_level_ref")
ref_levels
```

## Reference Conditions

The reference condition is defined by the `cov_val_ref` argument, which takes a
vector of covariate name:reference value pairs. `df_forest_preprocess()` flags 
the rows in the dataset with the reference values of covariates with the logical
variable `is_ref` and labels `cov_var` and `cov_val` as `"Reference"`.

```{r}
ref <- filter(simsum, is_ref == TRUE)
unique(ref$cov_var)
unique(ref$cov_val)
unique(ref$FOOD)
unique(ref$WTBL)
```

Every other scenario must differ from the reference in a univariate manner 
(i.e., by exactly one covariate value), and that covariate becomes the 
rows `cov_var`, with its labeled value as `cov_val`. No scenario identifier 
column or separate lookup table is needed, as the covariate combination in the 
dataset defines the scenario.

Matching is on the character form of the value, so a numeric column and a 
character reference value still line up. A scenario that varies two covariates 
at once has no single covariate to attribute the change to, so it aborts. 
Factorial designs are out of scope.

```{r preprocess-factorial, error=TRUE}
factorial_sim <- data_sad_pkforest_sim
factorial_sim$FOOD[factorial_sim$ID == 6] <- 1   # 90 kg *and* fed

df_forest_preprocess(
  factorial_sim,
  metric_vars   = "AUC",
  cov_vars      = c("FOOD", "WTBL"),
  cov_val_ref = c(FOOD = 0, WTBL = 70)
)
```


## Ratios

Test-to-Reference ratios are derived automatically for each metric producing a 
within-replicate test/reference ratio named `<metric><ratio_suffix>`. 

Because the parameter set is shared across scenarios within a replicate, 
uncertainty common to both test and reference cancels in the ratio.

`ratio = FALSE` emits the absolute metrics alone, and `ratio_suffix` renames 
the ratio metrics.

```{r preprocess-ratio}
df_forest_preprocess(
  data_sad_pkforest_sim,
  metric_vars   = "AUC",
  cov_vars      = c("FOOD", "WTBL"),
  cov_val_ref = c(FOOD = 0, WTBL = 70),
  ratio_suffix  = "RAT"
) %>%
  distinct(metric)
```


## Labels

`cov_labels` accepts a list of key:value pairs to define labels for each 
covariate, one entry per covariate, or a labeling function applied to the 
values. A value with no label falls back to its character form with a warning, 
which is what happens below for the fed level.

```{r preprocess-labels}
df_forest_preprocess(
  data_sad_pkforest_sim,
  metric_vars   = "AUC",
  cov_vars      = c("FOOD", "WTBL"),
  cov_val_ref = c(FOOD = 0, WTBL = 70),
  cov_labels    = list(FOOD = c("0" = "Fasted"))
) %>%
  distinct(cov_var, cov_val)
```



# Computing summary statistics with `df_forest()`

`df_forest()` is the summary function which produces a class tagged object
ready for rendering as a forest plot. 

The only required argument is `data`. The column-name arguments default to the
conventions `df_forest_preprocess()` emits:

  + `metric_name_var`: column of metric names, default `metric`
  + `cov_name_var`: column of covariate names, default `cov_var`
  + `cov_level_var`: column of covariate levels, default `cov_val`
  + `metric_value_var`: column of metric values, default `value`

Every row of a `(metric, covariate, level)` group is aggregated, so no 
replicate index column (e.g., `SIM`) is needed.

```{r df-forest-obj}
forest_obj <- df_forest(simsum)
forest_obj
```

The `stats` slot holds one row per plotted point with the canonical columns
`est`, `lo`, `hi`, and `ci_label`. `is_ref` is also present to flag the 
reference rows. The data.frame is output in plotting order.

```{r df-forest-stats}
forest_obj$stats
```


## Adjusting the summary statistics

The summary can be customized with:

  + `ci`: confidence interval to return, default `0.9` based on the interval 
  recommended for bioequivalence assessment.
  + `sigdigits`: number of significant digits in `ci_label`, default `3`. 
  Trailing zeros are kept so every value carries the same number of digits.

```{r df-forest-obj-95ci}
df_forest(simsum, ci = 0.95, sigdigits = 2)
```


## Reference

Reference rows are found one of two ways. When the data carries a logical flag 
column (`is_ref`), that column identifies the reference. This is the pathway
used when`df_forest_preprocess()` is the entry point into the workflow. 

Otherwise `cov_name_ref` names the value of `cov_var` that marks the reference
condition, default `"Reference"`, but can be called anything, as in the 
example below.

Reference rows flagged with `is_ref=TRUE` are
drawn as an open circle and sorted to the top of the plot. 

```{r df-forest-flag}
renamed <- simsum
renamed$cov_var[renamed$is_ref] <- "Typical subject"
renamed$cov_val[renamed$is_ref] <- "70 kg, fasted"
df_forest(renamed)$stats %>%
  filter(metric == "AUCRATIO") %>%
  select(cov_var, cov_val, is_ref, ci_label)
```

`cov_level_ref` is a named vector mapping each covariate to the reference level 
of that covariate. When supplied, the reference row is copied into each named
covariate panel under that label and the standalone reference panel is dropped,
so every panel shows the reference alongside the varied levels.

```{r df-forest-dispersed}
forest_obj <- df_forest(simsum,
                        cov_level_ref = ref_levels)
forest_obj$stats %>%
  filter(metric == "AUCRATIO")
```

If the data does not have the `is_ref` logical or `is_ref` should be ignored, 
it can be switched off by passing:

  + `is_ref_var = NULL` 
  
This will ignore the flag column and forces the `cov_name_ref` string match. 

If the data has no reference at all, switch off both:

  + `cov_name_ref = NULL`
  + `is_ref_var = NULL`.

## Row order

Rows of  are drawn in order top to bottom, and the order is read from the input 
data rather than alphanumerically:

  + Covariate name panels follow their factor levels when the input columns are
  factors, otherwise they order in order of first appearance.  
  
  + Covariate value levels within an individual covariate follow the factor 
  levels when the input columns are factors. The order specified in
  `cov_level_var` wins when all labels are covered, including a dispersed 
  reference label. Else, labels carrying a number are automatically sorted in 
  ascending numeric order (e.g., `50 kg` above `90 kg`, `-20%` above `-5%`, 
  and `Weight 50 kg` and `Weight 90 kg`).

To control the order explicitly:

  + a priori set factor levels of `cov_val` before calling `df_forest()`
  + a posteriori reorder the rows of `df_forest_obj$stats` before plotting.
  
The example below reorders the levels of the unique covariate values in the 
pre-processed dataset output by `df_forest_preprocess` before passing to 
`df_forest` to the desired order of descending body weights.

```{r df-forest-order}
data_wt_desc <- simsum %>%
  mutate(cov_val = factor(cov_val, levels = c("Reference", "Fasted", "Fed",
                                              "90 kg", "80 kg", "70 kg", "60 kg", "50 kg")))

df_forest(data_wt_desc, cov_level_ref = ref_levels)$stats %>%
  filter(metric == "AUCRATIO") %>%
  select(cov_var, cov_val, is_ref, ci_label)
```

# Plotting with `plot_forest()`

`plot_forest()` is the top-level wrapper that bundles `df_forest()` and 
`plot_build_forest()`. 

It renders one metric per call specified by the `metric` argument. When the 
input data carrys only one metric, the `metric` argument does not need to be 
specified and the metric is selected automatically. 

The output is a `ggplot` object with one facet row per covariate, the covariate
level on the y-axis, and the `ci_label` text as a right-hand estimate column 
under a header built from `ci` (e.g. `Median [90% CI]`).

```{r plot-raw, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot_forest(simsum, metric = "AUCRATIO")
```

The vertical reference line defaults to `ref = "reference"`. Pass a number to 
place it elsewhere, or `NULL` to suppress it.

## The reference band

`ref_band` is a numeric vector of length 2 specifying the bounds of a shaded
reference interval. Its two values are read according to `ref_band_type`:

  + `"multiplicative"` (default): the band is `ref * ref_band`
  + `"additive"`: the band is `ref + ref_band`
  + `"absolute"`: the band is `ref_band`

A multiplicative band is symmetric only on a log axis, which can be applied
through the style with `style_forest(logx = TRUE)`, or by adding
`scale_x_log10()` onto the returned `ggplot` object.

```{r plot-band, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot_forest(simsum, metric = "AUCRATIO",
            cov_level_ref = ref_levels,
            ref_band = c(0.8, 1.25),
            style = style_forest(logx = TRUE))
```
## Absolute exposure metrics

The same call works for an absolute metric. The reference line resolves to the
reference virtual participant's exposure, and a multiplicative band of
`c(0.8, 1.25)` scales with it, so the plot reads the same way as the ratio plot
but on the exposure scale. The intervals are wider than for the ratio.

```{r plot-absolute, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot_forest(simsum, metric = "AUC",
            cov_level_ref = ref_levels,
            ref_band = c(0.8, 1.25),
            style = style_forest(logx = TRUE))
```

## Difference metrics

Metrics on an additive scale, such as percent change from the reference, 
can be negative or zero, so they need a linear axis and an additive band. 

The example derives a percent-change metric from the ratio draws and brackets 
the reference change of zero with the equivalent of the 0.8 to 1.25 bounds.

```{r plot-additive, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
data_pchg <- simsum %>%
  filter(metric == "AUCRATIO") %>%
  mutate(metric = "AUCPCHG", value = 100 * (value - 1))

plot_forest(data_pchg,
            cov_level_ref = ref_levels,
            ref_band = c(-20, 25), ref_band_type = "additive")
```

## The estimate column header

The header above the estimate column is built from `ci` (`Median [90% CI]`). 
It is the plot tag, so it can be relabelled after the fact with `labs()`. 

For a ratio metric the conventional label names the quantity rather than the 
statistic, as in the example below

```{r plot-tag, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot_forest(simsum, metric = "AUCRATIO",
            cov_level_ref = ref_levels,
            ref_band = c(0.8, 1.25),
            style = style_forest(logx = TRUE)) +
  labs(tag = "Ratio [90% CI]")
```

## Reusing precomputed stats

`plot_forest()` also accepts a `forest_stats` object directly. 
This skips the aggregation and is the natural way to render several metrics 
from one summary, or to try different `ref_band` and `style` settings on the 
same data.

```{r plot-precomputed, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot_forest(forest_obj, metric = "CMAXRATIO", ref_band = c(0.8, 1.25),
            style = style_forest(logx = TRUE))

plot_forest(forest_obj, metric = "CMAX", ref_band = c(0.8, 1.25),
            style = style_forest(logx = TRUE))
```

When `data` is a precomputed `forest_stats` result, the pipeline arguments 
(`metric_name_var`, `cov_name_var`, `cov_level_var`, `metric_value_var`, `ci`,
`sigdigits`, `cov_name_ref`, `cov_level_ref`, `is_ref_var`) **cannot** be 
honored in `plot_forest` — those decisions were already made when `df_forest()`
ran. 

Passing any of these arguments aborts with a message pointing the caller back 
at `df_forest()`. Only the plot-only arguments (`metric`, `ref`, `ref_band`, 
`ref_band_type`,  `style`) are accepted on this path. 

# Inspecting the `forest_stats` object

`df_forest()` returns a `forest_stats` [`pmx_stats`][is_pmx_stats] object with 
three slots:

  + `stats` (one row per plotted point, in display order)
  + `obs` (always `NULL`; the forest family has no scatter overlay)
  + `config` (column names and summary configuration)

The returned object is class-tagged `c("forest_stats", "pmx_stats")`, which 
provides three S3 methods designed for interactive inspection.

`print()` shows a focused summary — object dimensions, the configuration values
(`metric_name_var`, `cov_name_var`, `cov_level_var`, `ci`), and the per-row 
stats body.

```{r print-stats}
print(forest_obj)
```

`summary()` shares the header but condenses the body to one line per row using
the metric and covariate level.

```{r summary-stats}
summary(forest_obj)
```

`as.data.frame()` returns the `stats` slot as a plain `data.frame`. The run 
configuration remains accessible via `forest_obj$config`.

```{r as-data-frame-stats}
plain <- as.data.frame(forest_obj)
class(plain)
forest_obj$config$cov_level_ref
```

Use `is_forest_stats()` to test class membership programmatically. 
Pass `strict = TRUE` to additionally validate structural integrity.

```{r predicate-stats}
is_forest_stats(forest_obj)
is_forest_stats(plain)  # FALSE -- coerced to a plain data.frame
```

# Styling

Plot aesthetics are customized via the `style` argument and the `style_forest()`
preset, which returns a `ggstylekit::style_spec()`. The series roles are:

  + `point` — the point estimate
  + `errorbar` — the confidence interval line
  + `ref_point` — the reference row's estimate (an open circle by default)
  + `ref_line` — the vertical reference line
  + `ref_band` — the shaded equivalence band (`fill` and `alphas`)

```{r style-defaults}
style_forest()
```

A typical override example is provided below using the style to change the
point sizes and the colors of the reference line and band:

```{r plot-styled, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot_forest(forest_obj, metric = "AUCRATIO", ref_band = c(0.8, 1.25),
            style = style_forest(shapes = c(point = 18),
                                 sizes = c(point = 3),
                                 colors = c(ref_line = "firebrick"),
                                 fill = c(ref_band = "steelblue"),
                                 alphas = c(ref_band = 0.15),
                                 logx = TRUE))
```

## Per-covariate coloring

Coloring by covariate is opt-in through the same `colors` map: add entries 
keyed by covariate name. 

When at least one plotted covariate is named, points and error bars are colored 
by covariate and the legend is suppressed, since the panel strips already label
each covariate. Covariates without an entry render in grey with a warning.

```{r plot-colored, fig.height=4, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot_forest(forest_obj, metric = "AUCRATIO", ref_band = c(0.8, 1.25),
            style = style_forest(colors = c(FOOD = "darkgreen", WTBL = "darkblue"),
                                 logx = TRUE))
```

The facet layout is fixed by the renderer (`facet_grid()` rows by covariate, 
strips outside the y-axis), so the style's `facet*` fields are ignored. 

The estimate column is right-hand axis text styled through the theme's 
`axis.text.y.right` element, and its header is the plot tag (`plot.tag`).

For a deeper treatment of the styling system — `style_spec()` fields, 
per-role maps, and post-hoc `restyle_plot()` / `reveal()` — see the 
[Plot Styling and Aesthetics](plot-styling.html) vignette.
